questions.question: A satellite circles Earth in an orbit with an inclination of 140°. What kind of orbit is it?
options: Retrograde: it moves westward, against Earth's rotation
Prograde: every inclination below 180° moves eastward
Polar: every inclination above 90° passes over the poles
Prograde, inclined 40° to the equator
questions.explanation: Inclinations between 90° and 180° are retrograde. Prograde means below 90°, and polar means at or close to 90°. Reading 180° minus 140° = 40° as the inclination of an eastward orbit confuses the angle with its supplement.

questions.section: What a launch has to deliver
questions.question: For a launch from the equator, due east, into an equatorial orbit, the delta-V is the orbit speed minus the speed of the launch site. Why may the two magnitudes be subtracted here?
options: Because the two velocity vectors point the same way
Because velocity is a scalar, so speeds always subtract
Because the speed of the site is small compared with the orbit speed
Because the target orbit is circular
questions.explanation: The vehicle must add the vector vorbit minus vsite. Only when the two are parallel does the magnitude of the difference equal the difference of the magnitudes. Velocity is a vector; a small or circular case does not change that.

questions.question: A vehicle launches from latitude 25° N toward azimuth 300°. With ωRE = 0.4646 km/s, what is ΔVrot?
questions.explanation: ΔVrot = ωRE cos φ sin Az = 0.4646 × cos 25° × sin 300° = −0.365 km/s: a westward launch loses speed. +0.365 drops the sign of sin 300°, +0.211 uses cos Az instead of sin Az, and −0.402 leaves out cos φ.

questions.question: What is the lowest orbit inclination a vehicle can reach by a direct launch from a site at latitude 34° N?
options: 34°, with a launch due east
0°, with the right choice of azimuth
56°, which is 90° minus the latitude
90°, since only a polar orbit passes over the site
questions.explanation: From cos i = cos φ sin Az and sin Az ≤ 1, cos i ≤ cos φ, so i ≥ φ; the minimum comes at Az = 90°. No azimuth gives 0°. 56° confuses the latitude with its complement, and many inclinations besides 90° pass over the site.

questions.section: Worked example: launch from a site at 30.4° N
questions.question: A site at latitude 20° N must launch directly into an orbit inclined at 50°. Which launch azimuths do it?
options: 43.2° only
None: 50° is out of reach from 20° N
questions.explanation: sin Az = cos 50° / cos 20° = 0.6840, so Az = 43.2° or 180° − 43.2° = 136.8°. Stopping at the calculator's one answer misses the southeast root. 46.8° comes from solving for cos Az instead of sin Az. The target is reachable because 50° is above the latitude.

questions.question: Why can a launch directly into the orbit plane of a space station happen only at certain times of day?
options: The turning site passes through the fixed orbit plane only twice a day
Earth's rotation speed changes over the day, so the rotation gain is right only at certain hours
The station must be directly above the launch site at liftoff
The launch range allows each azimuth only at one time of day
questions.explanation: The site rotates with Earth while the plane stays fixed among the stars; a direct launch is possible only as the site crosses the plane, which defines the launch window. Earth's rotation rate is constant, the station need not be overhead, and azimuth limits do not depend on the time of day.

questions.question: Why does a launch vehicle turn toward the horizontal early instead of climbing straight up to the orbit altitude first?
options: A long vertical climb makes the gravity loss grow
A vertical climb has the largest drag loss
A vertical climb has the largest steering loss
Gravity loss is zero in a vertical climb, so the turn is needed to use it
questions.explanation: Each second at flight-path angle γ costs g sin γ, which is largest when climbing vertically. A vertical climb leaves the dense air fastest, so it has the smallest drag loss, and it needs no steering. The gravity loss of a vertical climb is at its largest, not zero.

questions.question: A launch to a low circular orbit needs vorbit = 7.65 km/s, has losses of 1.8 km/s, and gains ΔVrot = 0.35 km/s from Earth's rotation. What is ΔVtotal?
questions.explanation: ΔVtotal = vorbit + ΔVlosses − ΔVrot = 7.65 + 1.8 − 0.35 = 9.10 km/s. 9.80 adds the rotation gain instead of subtracting it, 7.30 leaves out the losses, and 9.45 leaves out the rotation.
